title: How to introduce yourself: Easy English Conversations, Episode 1

notes.summary: Four people — Tim, Sian, Georgie and Buli — meet for the first time. They say hello, ask each other's names and say it's nice to meet. Then they practise talking about other people's names.

expressions.meaning: the question to ask someone's name
expressions.example: Hi, I'm Ana. What's your name?

expressions.meaning: two ways to say your name; "I'm" is more common when speaking
expressions.example: Hello, I'm Leo. / My name's Leo.

expressions.meaning: a friendly thing to say when you meet someone for the first time
expressions.example: Nice to meet you, Sam.

expressions.expression: Lovely / Great to meet you too.
expressions.meaning: the answer to "Nice to meet you"; add "too"
expressions.example: — Nice to meet you. — Great to meet you too.

expressions.meaning: a casual way to say "How are you?"
expressions.example: Hey, Tom! How's it going?

expressions.meaning: very informal ways to say hello, used with friends
expressions.example: Hiya! Are you coming to class?

expressions.meaning: use "his" for a man and "her" for a woman
expressions.example: This is my friend. Her name's Maya.

listen_for.note: The basic pattern: "What's your name?" → "I'm Tim." Notice "What's" sounds like one short word.
"My name's Tim." The 's is short and quick — you hardly hear it.
Different ways to say hello: Hello, Hi, Hey, Hiya. Which ones sound more relaxed?
Talking about other people: "What's his name?" and "What's her name?"
Different ways to say goodbye: Bye, Goodbye, Oh, bye!

questions: What are the names of the four people?
What do you say after someone says "Nice to meet you"?
Which greeting is more casual: "Hello" or "Hiya"?
Do you use "his" or "her" for Georgie?
notes.speaking_prompt: Imagine you meet someone new in your English class. Say hello, say your name, ask their name and say it's nice to meet them. Then introduce a friend or family member: "This is… His/Her name's…"

title: How to talk about your daily routine: Easy English Conversations, Episode 4
How to talk about your feelings: Easy English Conversations, Episode 14
Talking about lunch: Real Easy English

notes.summary: Beth and Neil are recording just before lunch, so they're both very hungry. They talk about what they brought today, what they usually eat, whether they ever skip meals, their favourite meal of the day, and eating at their desk.

expressions.meaning: I'm very, very hungry (informal, not literal)
expressions.example: Can we eat now? I'm starving.

expressions.meaning: food from an earlier meal that you didn't finish and eat later
expressions.example: I'm having last night's leftovers for lunch.

expressions.meaning: make cold food warm again
expressions.example: I'll heat up the soup in the microwave.

expressions.meaning: choose something
expressions.example: I usually go for the chicken salad.

expressions.meaning: not eat a meal
expressions.example: I was late, so I skipped breakfast.

expressions.meaning: angry because you're hungry (hungry + angry, informal)
expressions.example: Don't talk to me before lunch — I get hangry.

expressions.meaning: eating lunch while you work, often at your desk
expressions.example: We had a working lunch to finish the project.

expressions.meaning: I would prefer to…
expressions.example: I'd rather have rice than bread.

listen_for.note: Natural reactions: "I'm hungry." "Me too. I'm starving." Short answers like "Me too" keep a conversation going.
"Oh, that sounds really nice." A friendly way to react to what someone tells you.
Beth asks "What are leftovers?" — a useful way to ask about a word you don't know. Listen to how Neil explains it.
"What do you usually have for lunch?" → "It's usually…" Present simple for habits.
"Do you ever skip lunch?" "No. No way!" — strong, natural disagreement.
"No. Me neither." How to agree with a negative sentence (not "me too").

questions: What did Beth and Neil bring for lunch today?
What does Beth usually buy when she goes out for lunch?
Why does Neil never skip lunch?
What is Neil's favourite meal of the day, and why?
What does "I'd rather" mean? Make one sentence about food with it.
notes.speaking_prompt: What do you usually have for lunch on a work or school day? Do you bring food from home or buy it? Have you ever skipped lunch — how did you feel? Talk for one minute.

The benefits of doing nothing | 6 Minute English

notes.summary: Neil has had a busy day, but Beth has been relaxing. They discuss why many animals — even hard-working ants — spend most of their time doing nothing, and hear from a psychologist who thinks boredom can be good for us. There's also a quiz question about the slowest animal on Earth.

expressions.meaning: stop doing things and relax completely
expressions.example: On Sundays I just kick back and watch films.

expressions.meaning: very busy
expressions.example: She's been as busy as a bee getting ready for the party.

expressions.meaning: moving or travelling, not staying still
expressions.example: With three kids, we're always on the move.

expressions.expression: work up the energy (to do something)
expressions.meaning: slowly find enough energy or motivation to do something
expressions.example: I finally worked up the energy to clean the kitchen.

expressions.meaning: relax lazily, doing very little
expressions.example: We spent the holiday lounging about by the pool.

expressions.meaning: teach someone something useful, often surprisingly
expressions.example: My grandmother could teach you a thing or two about cooking.

expressions.meaning: thought to be better or more important than it really is
expressions.example: In my opinion, that restaurant is overrated.

expressions.meaning: stop worrying or thinking about something and relax
expressions.example: I find it hard to switch off after work.

listen_for.note: "Phew!" and a list with "then… then…" — a natural way to show you've had a busy day.
"It may not look it, but…" — a useful way to say appearances are wrong.
How a quiz question is asked with options a), b), c) — and how Neil answers: "Well, I think it's…"
A real expert speaking naturally, with fillers like "you know" and "kind of". It's faster — just try to get the main idea.
A question to the listener: "Would you get out of bed on Monday morning if you didn't have to?" Notice the second conditional.
The recap: each word is repeated with a short definition. Pause the video and try to remember the meaning before they say it.

questions: Why is Neil exhausted, and what has Beth been doing?
What surprising fact do scientists find when they look into an ant colony?
Give one possible reason why so many ants are inactive.
Why does Dr Sandi Mann think boredom can be useful?
What is the slowest animal on Earth, and how slowly does it move?
notes.speaking_prompt: Do you find it easy or hard to switch off and do nothing? Describe what you do when you want to kick back, and say whether you think being bored sometimes is good or bad for people.

title: Conversations with Retired People: Life Advice | Easy English 226
3 tips on how to study effectively

notes.summary: The video starts with a study of trainee surgeons: two groups learned the same skill, but one remembered it much better a month later. It explains how memories move from short-term to long-term storage, then gives three study techniques that work with the brain instead of against it.

expressions.expression: a matter of life and death
expressions.meaning: extremely important, because the result could be very serious
expressions.example: Getting to the airport on time isn't a matter of life and death, so relax.

expressions.meaning: because of what was just said; used to connect a reason to what comes next
expressions.example: The shop closes early on Sundays. With this in mind, let's go on Saturday.

expressions.meaning: explain something step by step so it's easier to understand
expressions.example: Let me unpack what the manager meant in that email.

expressions.meaning: a feeling that you're good or safe when you really aren't
expressions.example: Reading the answers gave me a false sense of confidence before the test.

expressions.meaning: think very hard to remember or solve something
expressions.example: I racked my brain, but I couldn't remember her name.

expressions.meaning: uses something earlier as a base and adds more to it
expressions.example: This week's lesson builds on what we learned about past tenses.

expressions.meaning: study a lot in a very short time, usually just before an exam
expressions.example: I stayed up all night cramming for my driving theory test.

expressions.meaning: stay somewhere (here: stay in your memory) for a long time
expressions.example: New words only stick around if you use them.

listen_for.note: How the narrator sets up a mystery: two groups, the same materials, one small change. Notice she doesn't tell you the answer yet.
"Let's first unpack…" — a natural way to say you're going to explain the background before the main point.
The contrast between what students prefer and what actually works. Listen for how "But" and "however" signal the turn.
The key term "interleaving" is introduced and immediately explained in simpler words. Notice the pattern: term, then "or…" + a plain explanation.
A question inside a sentence — "won't the material be fresh in your mind?" — used to show the listener's likely objection before answering it.
The ending returns to the surgeons from the start. This "full circle" structure is common in talks and presentations.

questions: What was different about the group of surgeons who performed better?
Why can rereading and highlighting give you a false sense of competence?
Why might making mistakes while testing yourself actually help you learn?
What is interleaving, and why does it work?
The narrator often explains a hard word with "or" followed by simpler words. Find one example.
notes.speaking_prompt: How do you usually study or learn new things — including English? After watching, which of the three techniques would you try, and how exactly would you use it this week?

Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance | Angela Lee Duckworth

notes.summary: A former maths teacher turned psychologist explains why she stopped believing that intelligence is what separates successful people from the rest. She describes her research in very different places — a military academy, a spelling competition, tough schools, sales teams — and names the one quality that kept predicting success, before admitting how little we know about building it.

expressions.meaning: the thing I noticed that surprised me or made a strong impression
expressions.example: What struck me was how quiet the city was on a Monday morning.

expressions.meaning: that made me start thinking seriously about something
expressions.example: My friend quit her job to travel, and that got me thinking about my own plans.

expressions.expression: I came to the conclusion that…
expressions.meaning: after thinking for a long time, I decided that…
expressions.example: After three months, I came to the conclusion that the course wasn't for me.

expressions.meaning: leave a school, course or programme before finishing it
expressions.example: He dropped out of university in his second year.

expressions.meaning: continue doing something even when it's difficult
expressions.example: Learning the guitar was hard at first, but I stuck with it.

expressions.meaning: every day, continuously, for a long time
expressions.example: She practised the piano day in, day out for years.

expressions.meaning: something that needs steady effort over a long time, not a short burst
expressions.example: Paying off a loan is a marathon, not a sprint.

expressions.meaning: do what you promised or planned to do
expressions.example: It's easy to make New Year's resolutions, but hard to follow through on them.

listen_for.note: A strong personal opening: a surprising career change in one sentence. Notice the contrast "demanding… even more demanding".
"But what if…?" — a question used to challenge a common belief. A very useful pattern for presenting an opinion.
Listen to the build-up: three things it wasn't, then the answer in two short words. Notice how she slows down and pauses before the key word.
Repetition as a speaking technique: "Grit is… Grit is… Grit is…" and "not just for the week, not just for the month, but for years".
"The honest answer is, I don't know." A natural, confident way to admit uncertainty — and the audience laughs. Notice the timing.
How she ends: "that's where I'm going to end my remarks, because that's where we are" — then a memorable final line that plays with the word gritty.

questions: Why did the speaker leave teaching to become a psychologist?
Name three of the settings where her team studied who would be successful.
How does she define grit? Try to explain it in your own words.
What did she find about the relationship between talent and grit?
What is a growth mindset, and why might it help people become grittier?
notes.speaking_prompt: Tell me about something you've stuck with for a long time even when it was hard — a job, a skill, a sport, learning English. What kept you going, and would you describe yourself as gritty? Why or why not?
